analysis.one_liner: Requires social media platforms to build safety controls for minors and undergo independent audits.
analysis.headline: The House subcommittee advanced the bill 13–10 on December 11, 2025; it now waits on the full Energy and Commerce Committee, and no version has reached the House floor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require popular social media apps to give minors tools to limit contact from strangers, time spent, and compulsive features like infinite scrolling, and to give parents tools to manage a child's account. Platforms would have to adopt policies against threats, sexual exploitation, drug sales, gambling, and deceptive financial harms to minors, block ads for those products aimed at minors, respond to harm reports within 10 days, and submit to annual independent third-party audits reported to the Federal Trade Commission. The FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the rules, but families themselves could not sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Minors and their parents gain the most: platforms must default to the most protective privacy and safety settings for users known to be minors, must turn parental tools on by default for children under 13, must let users and parents limit who can contact them and how much time is spent, and must flag advertising endorsements aimed at minors [S2]. Families also gain a fast reporting channel for harms to minors, with a substantive response due within 10 days [S2]. Parents of existing child accounts keep the choice to opt out of default parental tools if the platform notified them beforehand [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must give users they know are minors easy safeguards to limit contact from others, limit design features that cause compulsive use, and cap time on the app, with defaults set to the most protective option offered [S2].

Platforms must provide parental tools — viewing and (for children under 13) controlling privacy settings, restricting purchases, and viewing and limiting screen time — enabled by default for children's accounts [S2].

Platforms must adopt and enforce reasonable policies against threats of violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, drugs, tobacco, cannabis, gambling, and alcohol reaching minors, and cannot advertise those products to minors they know about [S2].

Every covered platform must undergo an annual independent third-party audit covering minor users, time spent, safeguards used, report handling, and data collection on minors, with results submitted to the FTC [S2].
The FTC can enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of residents for injunctions, damages, and restitution [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on social media and other interactive platforms covered by the bill: they must build and maintain safeguards, parental tools, and reporting systems, redesign engagement-driving features for minors, contract independent auditors annually, and face FTC and state enforcement. Section 9(c) says the bill does not require collecting age information the platform is not already collecting, and the duties attach to users the platform knows are minors, so the cost also depends on how aggressively platforms identify minors [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media and consumer internet platforms

drawbacks.text: Section 10 preempts state laws 'relating to the provisions of this Act', which could block states — including states that have already passed their own online safety laws — from enforcing stricter rules than this federal baseline [S2].

The bill requires no age verification: platforms need not collect age information they do not already gather, and most duties attach only to users the platform knows are minors, so a platform can limit its obligations by not knowing who its minor users are [S2].

Section 3 requires only 'reasonable' policies scaled to each platform's size and technical feasibility, and the bill sets no technical standard for what counts as adequate, giving platforms wide discretion in what they actually implement [S2].

Enforcement runs through the FTC and state attorneys general only; the bill gives families no private right of action, so a parent who believes a platform failed their child cannot sue directly under this law [S2].

Civil-liberties and LGBTQ advocacy groups argued earlier versions of this bill could pressure platforms into removing lawful content about topics like gender identity to avoid enforcement; this version adds language barring enforcement based on viewpoint and protecting minors' searches for information about the listed harms [S2], but the concern remains a real objection to the framework.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For families, the upside is real but modest: the bill mandates tools, defaults, response deadlines, and annual audits rather than holding platforms liable for harm, and it leaves a known gap — no age verification requirement — that platforms could use to keep their duties narrow. The most significant cost to the public is the federal preemption clause, which caps state-level protections at this federal floor. Compared with earlier versions of this legislation considered in the previous Congress, the duty-of-care provision that would have let regulators challenge harmful platform design directly is absent from this text. An honest supporter would say this is a floor-building bill, not a fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2025, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, marked up in the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade subcommittee five days later, and advanced to the full committee on a narrow 13–10 vote, where it has sat since with no committee vote, no floor action, and no cosponsors listed.

narrative.text: Rep. Gus Bilirakis introduced the bill in the House on December 5, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
The bill lists zero cosponsors on Congress.gov [S3].

On December 11, 2025, the Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee, in the nature of a substitute and amended, by a 13–10 vote [S4].
No further action — full committee vote, Rules Committee, or floor vote — appears in the action history as of the record provided [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the platforms: no federal rules have taken effect, the bill has no cosponsors and advanced its only vote 13–10, and platforms remain free to operate engagement-maximizing designs for minors while the bill waits in committee. Families with children on social media are no better off yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Platforms, for now — no new rules apply

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote is the subcommittee's 13–10 tally, which the record does not break down by party; the bill has a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors listed so far [S4][S3].

industries.industry: Social media and consumer internet platforms
industries.note: The bill forces platforms to build safeguards, default protections, reporting systems, and annual audits for minor users, and subjects them to FTC and state attorney general enforcement — a direct cost to engagement-driven business models that profit from time spent online. But it also preempts state online safety laws and sets duties only for users the platform 'knows' is a minor, so platforms gain a federal ceiling that caps stricter state rules.

industries.industry: Third-party parental-control and safety software vendors
industries.note: The bill expressly allows platforms to contract third parties whose primary function is providing the required safeguards and parental tools, creating a market for compliance services.
Every covered platform must commission an annual independent third-party audit and report results to the FTC, creating recurring audit demand.

analysis.trajectory: The bill's only recorded vote — 13–10 in subcommittee — signals a closely divided committee, and it lists no cosponsors, which historically makes reaching the House floor difficult. A version of this legislation passed the Senate 91–3 in the previous Congress but never received a House floor vote, so the House has been the choke point before. With the full Energy and Commerce Committee yet to act and floor time scarce, the realistic path is either a full committee markup if the chairman schedules one, or the bill sitting until the Congress ends in early 2027.
